claim: Meiotic cells undergo a single round of DNA replication followed by two rounds of chromosome segregation to produce haploid gametes.
source: Meiotic cells undergo a single round of DNA replication followed by two rounds of chromosome segregation (the meiotic divisions) to produce haploid gametes.
evidence: This is a fundamental description of meiosis stated in the abstract.

claim: CDK and the meiosis-specific kinase Ime2 cooperatively inhibit helicase loading.
source: CDK and the meiosis–specific kinase Ime2 cooperatively inhibit helicase loading, and their simultaneous inhibition allows inappropriate helicase reloading.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that simultaneous inhibition of both kinases results in helicase reloading.

claim: Simultaneous inhibition of CDK and Ime2 allows inappropriate helicase reloading.
source: CDK and the meiosis–specific kinase Ime2 cooperatively inhibit helicase loading, and their simultaneous inhibition allows inappropriate helicase reloading.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5D.

claim: CDK and the polo-like kinase Cdc5 trigger degradation of Sld2.
source: Finally, we show that CDK and the polo–like kinase Cdc5 trigger degradation of Sld2, an essential helicase–activation protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that mutation of CDK and Cdc5 phosphorylation sites on Sld2 results in protein stabilization.

claim: Sld2 is an essential helicase-activation protein.
source: Finally, we show that CDK and the polo–like kinase Cdc5 trigger degradation of Sld2, an essential helicase–activation protein.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the results section (Kamimura et al., 1998; Yeeles et al., 2015).

claim: Multiple kinases inhibit both helicase loading and activation between the meiotic divisions.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that multiple kinases inhibit both helicase loading and activation between the meiotic divisions, thereby ensuring reductive cell division.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by data showing CDK, Ime2, and Cdc5 all contribute to inhibiting DNA replication.

claim: ORC is bound to origins of replication throughout the meiotic divisions.
source: ORC is bound to origins of replication throughout the meiotic divisions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the figure legend and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mcm2-7 is bound to origins of replication in G1 phase but does not reassociate with origins during or between the meiotic divisions.
source: Mcm2–7 is bound to origins of replication in G1 phase but does not reassociate with origins during or between the meiotic divisions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the figure legend and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ORC was bound to a representative early-firing (ARS1) and late-firing (ARS1413) replication origin throughout both meiotic divisions.
source: Using ChIP–qPCR, we found that ORC was bound to a representative early–firing (ARS1) and late–firing (ARS1413) replication origin throughout both meiotic divisions (Figure 1B, top).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mcm2-7 was present at origins during pre-meiotic G1 phase but did not associate with either ARS1 or ARS1413 throughout MI and MII.
source: In contrast, although Mcm2–7 was present at origins during pre–meiotic G1 phase, this complex did not associate with either ARS1 or ARS1413 throughout MI and MII (Figure 1C, top).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ORC bound to ARS305 and ARS418 throughout the meiotic divisions.
source: As with the other origins tested, ORC bound to these origins throughout the meiotic divisions but Mcm2–7 loading was not observed after pre–meiotic G1 phase (Figure 1B and C, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mcm2-7 loading was not observed at ARS305 and ARS418 after pre-meiotic G1 phase.
source: As with the other origins tested, ORC bound to these origins throughout the meiotic divisions but Mcm2–7 loading was not observed after pre–meiotic G1 phase (Figure 1B and C, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mcm2-7 loading onto origins of replication is inhibited during the MI-MII transition.
source: Thus, Mcm2–7 loading onto origins of replication is inhibited during the MI–MII transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-qPCR data showing no Mcm2-7 binding during the MI-MII transition.

claim: Orc2 and Orc6 were not phosphorylated during G1 when CDK is inactive.
source: Consistent with robust helicase loading during pre–meiotic G1 phase (Figure 1C), Orc2 and Orc6 were not phosphorylated during G1 when CDK is inactive (Figure 2A and B) (Carlile and Amon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2A and 2B and cited reference (Carlile and Amon, 2008).

claim: Both Orc2 and Orc6 were phosphorylated throughout MI when CDK is highly active.
source: In contrast, both subunits were phosphorylated throughout MI when CDK is highly active.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Partial de-phosphorylation of both Orc2 and Orc6 was observed at the MI-MII transition.
source: Interestingly, we observed partial de–phosphorylation of both Orc2 (Figure 2A lane 9) and Orc6 (Figure 2B lane 6) at the MI–MII transition, before returning to a fully phosphorylated state that persisted until the end of MII.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Cdc6 protein was present during pre-meiotic G1 phase but became undetectable in MI when CDK is highly active.
source: We found that Cdc6 protein was present during pre–meiotic G1 phase but became undetectable in MI when CDK is highly active (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2C.

claim: Cdc6 protein partially reaccumulated during the MI-MII transition.
source: During the MI–MII transition, however, Cdc6 protein partially reaccumulated (Figure 2C lane 8) before decreasing again in MII.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2C.

claim: CDC6 mRNA was low during most of MI and MII but expression increased briefly during the MI-MII transition.
source: As with Cdc6 protein levels, although CDC6 mRNA was low during most of MI and MII, expression increased briefly during the MI–MII transition (Figure 2C lane 7).
evidence: This is supported by northern blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: Pre-treating helicase-loading proteins with purified Ime2 fully inhibited Mcm2-7 loading in vitro.
source: We found that pre-treating the helicase-loading proteins with purified Ime2 fully inhibited Mcm2–7 loading (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro helicase loading assay data in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Ime2 kinase activity is required for inhibition of Mcm2-7 loading.
source: In the presence of ATP, Ime2–AS inhibited Mcm2–7 loading to the same extent as wild–type (WT) Ime2 (compare Figure 3—figure supplement 1 to Figure 3C). However, the addition of 1–NA–PP1 to assays treated with Ime2–AS (but not WT Ime2) fully restored helicase loading (Figure 3D lanes 3–10).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro helicase loading assay data using analog-sensitive Ime2 and inhibitor in Figure 3D.

claim: Ime2-phosphorylation of one or more helicase-loading proteins directly inhibits origin licensing.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Ime2-phosphorylation of one or more helicase-loading proteins directly inhibits origin licensing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in vitro experiments showing Ime2 inhibits helicase loading using only purified proteins.

claim: Ime2 phosphorylation does not block the protein-protein interactions necessary for initial Mcm2-7 recruitment.
source: Thus, Ime2 phosphorylation does not block the protein–protein interactions necessary for initial Mcm2–7 recruitment, but instead must inhibit a downstream step during Mcm2–7 loading.
evidence: This is supported by OCCM complex formation assay data in Figure 3E showing Ime2 does not prevent OCCM formation.

claim: Ime2 phosphorylates Cdc6, Cdt1, and subunits of both ORC and the Mcm2-7 complex.
source: In vitro kinase assays showed that Ime2 phosphorylates Cdc6, Cdt1, and subunits of both ORC and the Mcm2–7 complex (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Mcm2-7 complex alone by Ime2 resulted in a >90% decrease in helicase loading.
source: Strikingly, we found that phosphorylation of the Mcm2–7 complex alone resulted in a >90% decrease in helicase loading (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro helicase loading assay data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Ime2 phosphorylation of ORC resulted in a ~50% reduction in helicase loading.
source: In contrast, Ime2 phosphorylation of ORC resulted in a ~50% reduction in loading, whereas reactions with phosphorylated Cdc6 and Cdt1 showed only minor defects (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro helicase loading assay data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: CDK only strongly inhibits ORC activity in helicase loading.
source: Although CDK also inhibits helicase loading in vitro, the equivalent experiment using CDK confirmed previous results showing that CDK only strongly inhibits ORC activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Chen and Bell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro helicase loading assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and cited reference (Chen and Bell, 2011).

claim: Ime2 phosphorylation of the Mcm2-7 complex is sufficient to inhibit helicase loading.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that Ime2 phosphorylation of the Mcm2–7 complex is sufficient to inhibit helicase loading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro experiments showing Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 alone causes >90% inhibition.

claim: The critical target required for direct inhibition of helicase loading is distinct between Ime2 and CDK.
source: Furthermore, although Ime2 and CDK both directly inhibit helicase loading, the critical target required for their direct inhibition is distinct.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the targets of Ime2 (Mcm2-7) and CDK (ORC) in helicase loading inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of CDK at the end of MI promoted only limited Mcm2-7 reloading and reaccumulation of CDC6 mRNA and protein.
source: Inhibition of CDK at the end of MI promoted only limited Mcm2–7 reloading and reaccumulation of CDC6 mRNA and protein, although ORC was substantially dephosphorylated in this condition (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5B showing limited effects of CDK inhibition alone.

claim: Ime2-inhibition only caused limited Mcm2-7 reloading.
source: Similar to CDK, however, Ime2-inhibition only caused limited Mcm2–7 reloading, although it did promote more significant reaccumulation of CDC6 mRNA and protein than CDK-inhibition (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5C showing limited effects of Ime2 inhibition alone.

claim: Neither CDK nor Ime2 are solely responsible for inhibiting helicase loading during the MI-MII transition.
source: Therefore, neither CDK nor Ime2 are solely responsible for inhibiting helicase loading during the MI–MII transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that inhibition of either kinase alone does not cause robust helicase reloading.

claim: Simultaneous inhibition of both CDK and Ime2 at the end of MI resulted in much higher levels of Mcm2-7 reloading than with either kinase alone.
source: Strikingly, simultaneous inhibition of both CDK and Ime2 at the end of MI resulted in much higher levels of Mcm2–7 reloading than we observe with either kinase alone (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5D showing robust helicase reloading upon co-inhibition.

claim: Co-inhibition of CDK and Ime2 restored expression of CDC6 mRNA and protein to levels observed in pre-meiotic G1 cells.
source: Furthermore, co–inhibition of these kinases restored expression of CDC6 mRNA and protein to levels observed in pre–meiotic G1 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and northern blot data in Figure 5D.

claim: Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within its phosphorylation-responsive degron domains in vitro.
source: Consistent with repression of Cdc6 by both kinases, mass spectrometry analysis showed that Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within its phosphorylation–responsive degron domains in vitro, and two of these sites directly overlap with CDK–sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1) (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 1, and cited references (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).

claim: Two Ime2 phosphorylation sites on Cdc6 directly overlap with CDK-sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation.
source: Consistent with repression of Cdc6 by both kinases, mass spectrometry analysis showed that Ime2 phosphorylates multiple sites on Cdc6 within its phosphorylation–responsive degron domains in vitro, and two of these sites directly overlap with CDK–sites known to contribute to Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1) (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and cited references (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).

claim: Neither CDK nor Ime2 is capable of full inhibition of helicase loading but together they are a potent inhibitor of origin licensing and CDC6 expression during the MI-MII transition.
source: Thus, neither CDK nor Ime2 is capable of full inhibition of helicase loading but together they are a potent inhibitor of origin licensing and CDC6 expression during the MI–MII transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vivo and in vitro data showing cooperative inhibition by both kinases.

claim: Most helicase-activation proteins were present throughout the meiotic divisions, including Cdc45, Psf2, Sld3, and Dpb11.
source: Most helicase–activation proteins were present throughout the meiotic divisions, including Cdc45, Psf2 (a member of the GINS complex), Sld3, and Dpb11 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sld2 was robustly degraded upon entry into MI and did not reaccumulate until the completion of MII.
source: In contrast, Sld2 was robustly degraded upon entry into MI and did not reaccumulate until the completion of MII (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6A.

claim: Sld2 is required to form the active eukaryotic replicative helicase, the Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS (CMG) complex.
source: Although helicase loading is an earlier event in replication initiation, we note that Sld2 is required to form the active eukaryotic replicative helicase, the Cdc45–Mcm2–7–GINS (CMG) complex (Heller et al., 2011; Kamimura et al., 1998; Muramatsu et al., 2010; Yeeles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations (Heller et al., 2011; Kamimura et al., 1998; Muramatsu et al., 2010; Yeeles et al., 2015).

claim: Mutation of either Cdc5-phosphorylation sites or CDK-phosphorylation sites on Sld2 results in stabilization of Sld2 throughout the meiotic divisions.
source: Mutation of either Cdc5–phosphorylation sites (sld2-2TA = T122A and T143A), CDK–phosphorylation sites (sld2-2SA = S128A and S138A), or both together (sld2-4A) resulted in stabilization of Sld2 during the meiotic divisions (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Both CDK- and Cdc5-phosphorylation are required to drive substantial Sld2 degradation.
source: Because both Sld2-2SA or Sld2-2TA were expressed at much higher levels than the WT protein during the meiotic divisions, both CDK– and Cdc5–phosphorylation are required to drive substantial Sld2 degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the levels of different Sld2 mutants in Figure 6E.

claim: CDK and Cdc5 inhibit Mcm2-7 activation during the meiotic divisions by promoting Sld2 degradation.
source: Together, these data indicate that CDK and Cdc5 inhibit Mcm2–7 activation during the meiotic divisions by promoting Sld2 degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing Sld2 degradation depends on CDK and Cdc5 phosphorylation sites.

claim: If an origin escapes the inhibition of Mcm2-7 loading during the meiotic divisions, Sld2 degradation would prevent activation of the associated helicases.
source: Thus, if an origin escapes the inhibition of Mcm2-7 loading during the meiotic divisions, Sld2 degradation would prevent activation of the associated helicases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional consequence of Sld2 degradation.

claim: Meiotic cells prevent DNA replication between the meiotic divisions using CDK, Ime2, and Cdc5 to inhibit both helicase loading and activation.
source: In this study, we address a fundamental question concerning the regulation of meiosis; how do meiotic cells undergo two sequential rounds of chromosome segregation without an intervening S–phase? We found that meiotic cells prevent DNA replication between the meiotic divisions using CDK, Ime2, and Cdc5 to inhibit both helicase loading and activation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Ime2 and CDK cooperate to inhibit helicase loading, and their co-inhibition was sufficient for aberrant origin licensing during the MI-MII transition.
source: Ime2 and CDK cooperate to inhibit helicase loading, and their co–inhibition was sufficient for aberrant origin licensing during the MI–MII transition.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5D showing robust helicase reloading upon co-inhibition.

claim: Unlike CDK, Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 directly inhibits its participation in helicase loading.
source: In particular, we found that unlike CDK, Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2–7 directly inhibits its participation in helicase loading.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro data in Figure 4 showing Ime2 phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 inhibits helicase loading.

claim: Meiotic cells use CDK and the polo-like kinase Cdc5 to promote degradation of Sld2.
source: In addition to the inhibition of origin licensing, meiotic cells use CDK and the polo–like kinase Cdc5 to promote degradation of Sld2, a key helicase-activation protein.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing Sld2 degradation depends on CDK and Cdc5 phosphorylation sites.

claim: Multiple kinases inhibit DNA replication between the two meiotic divisions by targeting both many components of the helicase-loading machinery and at least one helicase-activation protein.
source: Together, these data reveal that multiple kinases inhibit DNA replication between the two meiotic divisions by targeting both many components of the helicase-loading machinery and at least one helicase-activation protein.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The amount of CDK activity present during the MI-MII transition is sufficient to inhibit most origin licensing.
source: In support of the CDK–balance model, the amount of CDK activity present during the MI–MII transition is sufficient to inhibit most origin licensing, because Ime2 inhibition does not result in strong Mcm2–7 reloading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Ime2 inhibition alone does not cause robust helicase reloading.

claim: The decrease in CDK activity that resets the chromosome segregation program is not sufficient to fully reset the DNA replication program.
source: Thus, the decrease in CDK activity that resets the chromosome segregation program (Bizzari and Marston, 2011; Buonomo et al., 2003; Carlile and Amon, 2008; Fox et al., 2017; Marston et al., 2003) is not sufficient to fully reset the DNA replication program.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and supported by multiple citations (Bizzari and Marston, 2011; Buonomo et al., 2003; Carlile and Amon, 2008; Fox et al., 2017; Marston et al., 2003).

claim: CDK inhibition did not result in extensive Mcm2-7 reloading during the MI-MII transition.
source: In support of the alternative–kinase model, we found that CDK inhibition similarly did not result in extensive Mcm2–7 reloading during the MI-MII transition.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo data in Figure 5B showing limited effects of CDK inhibition alone.

claim: Two additional kinases contribute to the inhibition of DNA replication between the meiotic divisions: Ime2 inhibits helicase loading, and Cdc5 helps stimulate the degradation of Sld2.
source: Instead, we show that two additional kinases contribute to the inhibition of DNA replication between the meiotic divisions. Ime2 inhibits helicase loading, and Cdc5 helps stimulate the degradation of Sld2.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: The inhibition of DNA replication by Ime2 and Cdc5 allows for CDK to oscillate and reset the chromosome segregation program without allowing a new round of DNA replication.
source: The inhibition of DNA replication by Ime2 and Cdc5 allows for CDK to oscillate and reset the chromosome segregation program without allowing a new round of DNA replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Meiotic cells use Ime2 and Cdc5 to inhibit helicase loading and activation, respectively, suggesting that CDK-dependent inhibition of origin licensing is not adequate to ensure genome stability during meiosis.
source: That meiotic cells use Ime2 and Cdc5 to inhibit helicase loading and activation, respectively, suggests that CDK–dependent inhibition of origin licensing is not adequate to ensure genome stability during meiosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings that multiple kinases are required.

claim: A subset of the mechanisms by which CDK and Ime2 inhibit helicase loading are non-overlapping.
source: Furthermore, a subset of the mechanisms by which CDK and Ime2 inhibit helicase loading are non–overlapping, providing additional avenues to prevent inappropriate replication (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing different targets for CDK (ORC) and Ime2 (Mcm2-7).

claim: The transient weakening of both Cdc6 repression and ORC phosphorylation during the MI-MII transition indicates that the associated decrease in CDK activity is a significant threat to origin licensing.
source: The transient weakening of both Cdc6 repression and ORC phosphorylation during the MI–MII transition (Figure 2) indicates that the associated decrease in CDK activity (Carlile and Amon, 2008) is a significant threat to origin licensing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 2 and cited reference (Carlile and Amon, 2008).

claim: Ime2 has a larger role than CDK for Cdc6 repression at the MI-MII transition.
source: Even the additional repression of Cdc6 by Ime2 is not sufficient to fully eliminate the protein during the MI-MII transition, although Ime2 has a larger role than CDK for Cdc6 repression at this time (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of CDK and Ime2 inhibition on Cdc6 levels in Figure 5.

claim: Preventing DNA re-replication in meiotic cells is more important than in mitotic cells to ensure that the inherited genome remains intact in multicellular eukaryotes.
source: It is worth noting that in multicellular eukaryotes, preventing DNA re-replication in meiotic cells is more important than in mitotic cells to ensure that the inherited genome remains intact.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of preventing re-replication in meiosis.

claim: In mitotic cells, prevention of DNA re-replication relies on inhibiting Mcm2-7 loading.
source: In mitotic cells, prevention of DNA re–replication relies on inhibiting Mcm2–7 loading (Arias and Walter, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Arias and Walter, 2007).

claim: Sld2 degradation in mitotic cells is important for ensuring genome stability at the M-G1 transition, but not during other parts of the mitotic cell cycle.
source: Previous studies found that Sld2 degradation in mitotic cells is important for ensuring genome stability at the M–G1 transition, but not during other parts of the mitotic cell cycle (Reusswig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Reusswig et al., 2016).

claim: Mechanisms preventing DNA re-replication at the mitotic M-G1 transition also function during meiosis at the MI-MII transition.
source: Our finding that Sld2 is absent during both meiotic divisions suggests that mechanisms preventing DNA re–replication at the mitotic M–G1 transition also function during meiosis at the MI–MII transition, a partially G1-like state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Sld2 is degraded during meiotic divisions.

claim: Dbf4 is degraded during both mitotic anaphase and meiotic anaphase I.
source: Consistent with this idea, Dbf4, which binds to Cdc7 to form the kinase DDK and is also required for helicase activation, is degraded during both mitotic anaphase (Ferreira et al., 2000) as well as meiotic anaphase I (Matos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Ferreira et al., 2000; Matos et al., 2008).

claim: The degradation of Sld2 and Dbf4 strongly suggests that meiotic cells further protect themselves from replication initiation during the meiotic divisions by inhibiting multiple steps during Mcm2-7 activation.
source: The degradation of these two proteins strongly suggests that meiotic cells further protect themselves from replication initiation during the meiotic divisions by inhibiting multiple steps during Mcm2–7 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that multiple helicase activation proteins are degraded.

claim: Ime2 is not just a backup for the known inhibitory mechanisms used by CDK.
source: Ime2 is not just a backup for the known inhibitory mechanisms used by CDK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that Ime2 has distinct mechanisms of inhibition compared to CDK.

claim: Ime2 uses at least two mechanisms similar to CDK: Cdc6 degradation and Mcm2-7 nuclear export.
source: We found that in addition to using at least two mechanisms similar to CDK (Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5) (Drury et al., 2000) and Mcm2-7 nuclear export (Holt et al., 2007)), Ime2-phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 results in a distinct mechanism of inhibition not seen after CDK-phosphorylation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 4 and 5, and citations (Drury et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2007).

claim: Ime2-phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 results in a distinct mechanism of inhibition not seen after CDK-phosphorylation.
source: We found that in addition to using at least two mechanisms similar to CDK (Cdc6 degradation (Figure 5) (Drury et al., 2000) and Mcm2-7 nuclear export (Holt et al., 2007)), Ime2-phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 results in a distinct mechanism of inhibition not seen after CDK-phosphorylation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing Ime2 targets Mcm2-7 while CDK targets ORC.

claim: Previous studies have not identified a mechanism that directly prevents Mcm2-7 from completing helicase loading.
source: Origin licensing is inhibited by a number of different mechanisms across eukaryotic evolution, but previous studies have not identified a mechanism that directly prevents Mcm2-7 from completing helicase loading (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claim: The ability of Ime2 to inhibit helicase loading suggests an important role for this kinase during the meiotic G1-S transition.
source: The ability of Ime2 to inhibit helicase loading also suggests an important role for this kinase during the meiotic G1–S transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about Ime2's role in inhibiting helicase loading.

claim: During the mitotic G1-S transition, helicase loading is inhibited by G1-CDK before helicase activation is stimulated by S-phase CDK.
source: During the mitotic G1–S transition, helicase loading is inhibited by G1–CDK before helicase activation is stimulated by S–phase CDK (Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999).

claim: During meiosis, G1 cyclins are not expressed and it is Ime2 that triggers activation of S-CDK at the G1-S transition.
source: During meiosis, G1 cyclins are not expressed and it is Ime2 that triggers activation of S–CDK at the G1–S transition (Benjamin et al., 2003; Dirick et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Benjamin et al., 2003; Dirick et al., 1998).

claim: Ime2 can robustly inhibit helicase loading by multiple mechanisms, similar to G1-CDK.
source: Our data and previous studies (Holt et al., 2007) show that Ime2 can robustly inhibit helicase loading by multiple mechanisms, similar to G1-CDK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current data and cited previous study (Holt et al., 2007).

claim: Ime2 insulates helicase loading from helicase activation during the meiotic G1-S transition in an analogous manner to G1-CDK during the mitotic G1-S transition.
source: These observations strongly suggest that Ime2 insulates helicase loading from helicase activation during the meiotic G1–S transition in an analogous manner to G1–CDK during the mitotic G1–S transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Ime2's role in meiosis to G1-CDK's role in mitosis.

claim: The problem of uncoupling DNA replication and chromosome segregation during meiosis is conserved in other eukaryotes.
source: The problem of uncoupling DNA replication and chromosome segregation during meiosis is conserved in other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the conservation of this biological problem.

claim: Metazoans also use CDK to regulate both chromosome segregation and DNA replication.
source: Metazoans also use CDK to regulate both chromosome segregation and DNA replication (Arias and Walter, 2007; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claim: Metazoans mostly rely on CDK-independent mechanisms to inhibit Mcm2-7 loading during S and G2 phase.
source: Although metazoans mostly rely on CDK–independent mechanisms to inhibit Mcm2–7 loading during S and G2 phase, these mechanisms are not as potent during M–phase at which point Cdk1 becomes a critical inhibitor of origin licensing (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claim: Cdk1 becomes a critical inhibitor of origin licensing during M-phase in metazoans.
source: Although metazoans mostly rely on CDK–independent mechanisms to inhibit Mcm2–7 loading during S and G2 phase, these mechanisms are not as potent during M–phase at which point Cdk1 becomes a critical inhibitor of origin licensing (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Arias and Walter, 2007; Siddiqui et al., 2013).

claim: Transient inactivation of Cdk1 in human cells is sufficient for DNA re-replication, just as it is in yeast.
source: Transient inactivation of Cdk1 in human cells is sufficient for DNA re–replication, just as it is in yeast (Bates et al., 1998; Dahmann et al., 1995; Itzhaki et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Bates et al., 1998; Dahmann et al., 1995; Itzhaki et al., 1997).

claim: An oscillation of Cdk1 activity is required for correct chromosome segregation in mammalian cells.
source: An oscillation of Cdk1 activity is also required for correct chromosome segregation in mammalian cells (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009).

claim: Human Cdk2 can rescue some meiotic defects associated with ime2∆ in yeast.
source: Human Cdk2 can rescue some meiotic defects associated with ime2∆ in yeast (Szwarcwort-Cohen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Szwarcwort-Cohen et al., 2009).

claim: Cdk2 is not required for mitosis in mice, but it is required for both male and female meiosis.
source: Additionally, Cdk2 is not required for mitosis in mice, but it is required for both male and female meiosis (Ortega et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Ortega et al., 2003).

claim: Mammalian Cdk2 may have a similar role during meiosis as Ime2 does in yeast.
source: With regard to how DNA replication and chromosome segregation are uncoupled during mammalian meiosis, previous studies raise the intriguing possibility that mammalian Cdk2 may have a similar role during meiosis as Ime2 does in yeast.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the cited studies about Cdk2 and Ime2.

claim: During G1 phase, low CDK activity allows for the Mcm2-7 complex to be loaded onto origins of replication in an inactive state.
source: During G1 phase, low CDK activity allows for the Mcm2–7 complex, the core enzyme of the replicative helicase, to be loaded onto origins of replication in an inactive state.
evidence: This is a description of the mitotic cell cycle regulation stated in the introduction.

claim: Helicase loading cannot occur in the presence of high CDK activity.
source: This event, known as origin licensing or helicase loading, cannot occur in the presence of high CDK activity and requires the cooperative action of three proteins: Cdc6, Cdt1, and the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).

claim: Helicase loading requires the cooperative action of three proteins: Cdc6, Cdt1, and the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC).
source: This event, known as origin licensing or helicase loading, cannot occur in the presence of high CDK activity and requires the cooperative action of three proteins: Cdc6, Cdt1, and the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Evrin et al., 2009; Remus et al., 2009).

claim: S-CDK phosphorylates Sld2 and Sld3 to promote helicase activation, replisome assembly, and chromosome duplication.
source: Upon S–phase entry, S–CDK (CDK bound to S-phase cyclins Clb5/6) is activated and impacts DNA replication in two ways. First, S–CDK phosphorylates two essential proteins, Sld2 and Sld3, that subsequently promote helicase activation, replisome assembly, and chromosome duplication (Masumoto et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2007; Zegerman and Diffley, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Masumoto et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2007; Zegerman and Diffley, 2007).

claim: Both S-CDK and M-CDK inhibit new helicase loading during S, G2, and M phases.
source: Second, both S–CDK and M-CDK (CDK bound to mitotic cyclins Clb1-4) inhibit new helicase loading during S, G2, and M phases.
evidence: This is a description of CDK regulation stated in the introduction.

claim: CDK directly phosphorylates Cdc6, Mcm3, and ORC to trigger the proteolytic degradation of Cdc6, the nuclear export of Mcm2-7-Cdt1, and inhibition of ORC helicase-loading activity.
source: These kinases directly phosphorylate Cdc6, Mcm3, and ORC to trigger the proteolytic degradation of Cdc6, the nuclear export of Mcm2–7–Cdt1, and inhibition of ORC helicase–loading activity, respectively (Calzada et al., 2000; Chen and Bell, 2011; Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999; Nguyen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by multiple citations (Calzada et al., 2000; Chen and Bell, 2011; Drury et al., 2000; Labib et al., 1999; Nguyen et al., 2000).

claim: CDK oscillations ensure that chromosome segregation occurs once per mitotic cell cycle.
source: CDK oscillations also ensure that chromosome segregation occurs once per mitotic cell cycle (Winey and Bloom, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Winey and Bloom, 2012).

claim: G1-CDK is required for duplication of the SPB at the end of G1 phase.
source: At the end of G1 phase, G1–CDK (CDK bound to G1 cyclins Cln1-3) is required for duplication of the SPB (Jaspersen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Jaspersen et al., 2004).

claim: S-CDK and M-CDK prevent re-duplication of SPBs.
source: Later in the cell cycle, S–CDK and M–CDK prevent re–duplication of SPBs, and M-CDK is essential for the assembly of metaphase spindles (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).

claim: M-CDK is essential for the assembly of metaphase spindles.
source: Later in the cell cycle, S–CDK and M–CDK prevent re–duplication of SPBs, and M-CDK is essential for the assembly of metaphase spindles (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Avena et al., 2014; Elserafy et al., 2014; Haase et al., 2001).

claim: Downregulation of CDK activity is required for anaphase spindle disassembly upon completion of chromosome segregation.
source: Finally, downregulation of CDK activity is required for anaphase spindle disassembly upon completion of chromosome segregation (Shirayama et al., 1999; Thornton and Toczyski, 2003; Wäsch and Cross, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Shirayama et al., 1999; Thornton and Toczyski, 2003; Wäsch and Cross, 2002).

claim: The CDK-balance model suggests that partially inactivating CDK is sufficient to reset the chromosome segregation program while still inhibiting Mcm2-7 loading and replication initiation.
source: The CDK–balance model suggests that partially inactivating CDK is sufficient to reset the chromosome segregation program while still inhibiting Mcm2–7 loading and replication initiation (Iwabuchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of a model stated in the introduction and supported by citation (Iwabuchi et al., 2000).

claim: The alternative-kinase model suggests that a second kinase inhibits Mcm2-7 loading during the MI-MII transition.
source: In contrast, the alternative–kinase model suggests that a second kinase inhibits Mcm2–7 loading during the MI–MII transition, allowing the oscillation of CDK activity to reset the chromosome segregation program without resetting the DNA replication program.
evidence: This is a description of a model stated in the introduction.

claim: Ime2 has been proposed to inhibit Mcm2-7 loading during the MI-MII transition.
source: Ime2, a yeast meiosis–specific kinase that is evolutionarily related to CDK (Krylov et al., 2003), has been proposed to have this role (Holt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Krylov et al., 2003; Holt et al., 2007).

claim: Ime2 is a yeast meiosis-specific kinase that is evolutionarily related to CDK.
source: Ime2, a yeast meiosis–specific kinase that is evolutionarily related to CDK (Krylov et al., 2003), has been proposed to have this role (Holt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Krylov et al., 2003).

claim: Ime2 is active during the meiotic divisions.
source: Previous studies found that Ime2 is active during the meiotic divisions (Berchowitz et al., 2013) and that, like CDK, this kinase can promote Mcm2–7 nuclear export upon completion of meiotic S phase (Holt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Berchowitz et al., 2013).

claim: Ime2 can promote Mcm2-7 nuclear export upon completion of meiotic S phase.
source: Previous studies found that Ime2 is active during the meiotic divisions (Berchowitz et al., 2013) and that, like CDK, this kinase can promote Mcm2–7 nuclear export upon completion of meiotic S phase (Holt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation (Holt et al., 2007).

claim: Phosphorylation of Orc2 and Orc6 by CDK prevents ORC from facilitating helicase loading.
source: Phosphorylation of Orc2 and Orc6 by CDK prevents ORC from facilitating helicase loading (Chen and Bell, 2011; Nguyen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Chen and Bell, 2011; Nguyen et al., 2001).

claim: CDK-phosphorylation of Cdc6 targets it for proteolytic degradation.
source: Unlike ORC inhibition, CDK–phosphorylation of Cdc6 targets it for proteolytic degradation (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000) and CDK is also partially responsible for repression of CDC6 transcription (Moll et al., 1991; Piatti et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000).

claim: CDK is partially responsible for repression of CDC6 transcription.
source: Unlike ORC inhibition, CDK–phosphorylation of Cdc6 targets it for proteolytic degradation (Calzada et al., 2000; Drury et al., 2000) and CDK is also partially responsible for repression of CDC6 transcription (Moll et al., 1991; Piatti et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations (Moll et al., 1991; Piatti et al., 1995).

claim: Reduced CDK activity during the MI-MII transition results in a partial but detectable decrease of ORC phosphorylation and a slight reaccumulation of Cdc6.
source: Taken together, these findings suggested that reduced CDK activity during the MI–MII transition results in a partial but detectable decrease of ORC phosphorylation and a slight reaccumulation of Cdc6.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 2.

claim: Ime2 must inhibit a downstream step during Mcm2-7 loading after OCCM formation.
source: Thus, Ime2 phosphorylation does not block the protein–protein interactions necessary for initial Mcm2–7 recruitment, but instead must inhibit a downstream step during Mcm2–7 loading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OCCM formation assay data in Figure 3E.

claim: At least two of the CDK-dependent mechanisms preventing Mcm2-7 loading in mitotic cells were transiently weakened during the MI-MII transition.
source: We found that at least two of these mechanisms were transiently weakened during the MI–MII transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing partial ORC dephosphorylation and Cdc6 reaccumulation.

claim: ORC binding to DNA is not limiting for replication initiation during meiosis.
source: ORC binding to DNA is therefore not limiting for replication initiation during meiosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP-qPCR data showing ORC remains bound throughout meiosis.

claim: The lack of Mcm2-7 binding to origins was not due to the absence of Mcm2-7 proteins or the essential helicase-loading protein Cdt1.
source: The lack of Mcm2–7 binding to origins was not due to the absence of Mcm2–7 proteins or the essential helicase–loading protein Cdt1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both ORC and Mcm2-7 associated specifically with origin DNA sequences compared to non-origin DNA.
source: Both ORC and Mcm2-7 associated specifically with origin DNA sequences compared to non-origin DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mcm2-7 loading is the earliest inhibited step of replisome assembly during the MI-MII transition.
source: To address how DNA replication is inhibited between MI and MII, we sought to identify the earliest inhibited step of replisome assembly.
evidence: This is the main finding of the section, supported by the ChIP-qPCR data showing Mcm2-7 is not loaded while ORC remains bound.
